label: bad
seen: No measurement of this game exists; none was taken. I saw no score, band or tier of it or of its parent while building and labelling it; the parent's published verdicts in labelled-set.md §9 I did not open in this task.
claim: White wins by force: its king walks its road and arrives on a6 on White's sixth move, and no win for either side can come sooner.
change: two: every piece barred from the other side's road (d1, c2, b3, b4, a5, a6 for White, mirrored for Black), and `rules.reach` for the king on a6 (mirrored, a3, for Black).
aim: A player reading about four plies never sees five king steps ahead, and an evaluator has no reason to march its king off its back rank, so play should go as the parent's: decisive from both seats by mate and of ordinary length; the road matters only to a player who knows it is there.

proof.text: Every piece type carries `region` (the only squares it may ever occupy, written for White and mirrored for Black), so a piece may not move, take, promote or drop onto a square closed to it, and therefore never attacks such a square: a king standing on a square closed to every enemy piece is never in check. The region leaves out Black's road, so no black piece, its king included, may stand on or attack White's road d1, c2, b3, b4, a5, a6; `rules.reach` wins for a king arriving on a6 (a3 for Black). The forced win: White's first move is c2-c3, which empties the square the road leaves d1 by; then the king steps c2 - b3 - b4 - a5 - a6. Each step is onto an empty square of the road (no black piece may stand there, and no white piece is in the way) that no black piece attacks, so it is legal whatever Black has played, and the sixth move arrives on a6 and wins. Nothing sooner: d1 to a6 is five king steps and every square next to d1 holds a white piece (or a wall) at the start, so White's king cannot arrive before White's sixth move; White cannot mate sooner, since Black's king on d8 stands on Black's road and is never in check, and Black has other moves for its first five turns. Black's king is in the same box (d8 to a3 is five steps, every square next to it held by a piece or a wall), so Black cannot arrive before its own sixth move, which comes after White's, and it cannot mate White's king on White's road. Shatranj's stalemate (a loss) cannot touch White, which always has its road step. The line in `checks` is one legal game following the recipe.
